abq.name: Albuquerque
abq.text: Albuquerque lies in central New Mexico, straddling the Rio Grande between the Sandia and Manzano mountain ranges and bisected by historic Route 66. The settlement was founded in 1706 as Alburquerque, a Spanish colonial outpost that later grew into the state’s largest city. Today visitors can wander the colourful Old Town with its adobe churches and bustling markets, ride the world-famous hot-air balloons that dot the sky each October, explore the nearby mountains by tram or trail, and enjoy a lively mix of Southwestern cuisine, street art and modern museums, all set against a backdrop of striking desert-mountain scenery.

adz.name: Adana
adz.text: Adana, a major city in southern Turkey, sits on the banks of the Seyhan River about 70 kilometres inland from the Mediterranean coast. It has been an important centre since antiquity, serving as a key stop on the ancient trade routes of Cilicia and later becoming a thriving Ottoman provincial capital. Today the city is famous for its spicy kebabs, lively street markets and the impressive stone bridge of Taşköprü spanning the river. Visitors can explore the historic Great Mosque, wander the palm-lined riverfront promenade and enjoy the surrounding plains that produce some of the country’s finest citrus fruits.

aer.name: Sochi
aer.text: Sochi sits on the sunny shores of the Black Sea at the foot of the Caucasus mountains, in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai region, stretching over a narrow strip of coastline that feels both seaside and alpine. It first rose to prominence in the late-19th century as a health resort for the Russian aristocracy, and today it is perhaps best remembered for hosting the 2014 Winter Olympics, which transformed its infrastructure and skyline. Visitors can wander palm-lined promenades, take a cable-car up to the ski slopes of the nearby mountains, and enjoy a blend of modern hotels, lively cafés and historic Soviet-era architecture, all under a mild climate that makes it a year-round destination.

ahw.name: Ahvaz
ahw.text: Ahvaz sits on the banks of the Karun River in southwestern Iran, near the border with Iraq and the Persian Gulf. It is the capital of Khuzestan province and has long been a key centre for Iran’s oil industry, with the first oil well in the country drilled nearby in 1908. Today the city offers a striking mix of modern high-rises and traditional bazaars, while the wide river promenade provides a pleasant place to watch the flow of the Karun and enjoy local cafés serving spicy kebabs and sweet, rose-flavoured tea.

amb.name: Ambon
amb.text: Ambon—nestled in the heart of Indonesia’s Maluku archipelago, this emerald‑green island sits at the crossroads of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, where sparkling bays meet volcanic hills. Once the prized “Spice Islands,” Ambon thrived as a bustling hub for Dutch, Portuguese and local traders, its forts and colonial streets echoing centuries of maritime adventure. Today, the city buzzes with vibrant markets, world‑class diving sites teeming with manta rays, and a lively blend of cultures reflected in music, cuisine and festivals. From its historic fortifications to its thriving creative scene, Ambon invites travelers to explore a living tapestry of history, nature and modern Indonesian spirit.

amd.name: Ahmedabad
amd.text: Ahmedabad, situated in the western Indian state of Gujarat along the Sabarmati River, is a bustling metropolis famed for its rich heritage and vibrant street life. Founded in the 15th century by Sultan Ahmed Shah, the city’s historic walled centre, the Pol, still houses intricately carved havelis, bustling bazaars and the striking Jama Masjid. Today visitors can wander through the UNESCO-listed old city, savour delicious Gujarati thalis, explore the tranquil Sabarmati Ashram where Mahatma Gandhi once lived, and admire contemporary art at the Calico Museum, all amid a lively mix of modern cafés and colourful festivals.

ams.name: Amsterdam
ams.text: Amsterdam, the lively capital of the Netherlands, sits on the banks of the Amstel River and spreads across a network of historic canals that give the city its famous, picturesque charm. First granted city rights in 1300, it grew into a major trading hub during the Dutch Golden Age, when artists like Rembrandt and Vermeer worked in its bustling workshops. Today the streets are a mix of centuries-old gabled houses and modern cafés, with cyclists weaving between the canals, museums showcasing world-class art, and a relaxed, multicultural atmosphere that makes wandering the city feel both timeless and fresh.

ayt.name: Antalya
ayt.text: Antalya, a coastal city on Turkey’s southwestern Mediterranean shore, sits at the foot of the Taurus Mountains and enjoys a mild climate year-round. It has been a gateway to the ancient region of Pamphylia since Roman times, with the well-preserved ruins of Hadrian’s Gate marking the old city’s entrance. Today the promenade along Konyaaltı Beach is lined with cafés, boutique shops and lively street performers, while the historic Kaleiçi district offers winding lanes, Ottoman houses and rooftop terraces that overlook the sparkling sea, making a stroll feel both relaxed and full of discovery.

bal.name: Baltimore
bal.text: Baltimore sits on the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay in Maryland, about 40 miles north of Washington, D.C. It grew around the 1729 port that later became a major gateway for immigrants and a key Union supply line during the Civil War. Today the city blends historic charm with modern buzz: you can wander the cobbled streets of Fell’s Point, admire the striking Inner Harbor skyline, sample crab cakes at bustling waterfront restaurants, and explore world-class museums such as the American Visionary Art Museum. Friendly locals, lively music scenes and scenic waterfront walks make a visit both relaxed and memorable.

bcn.name: Barcelona
bcn.text: Barcelona, perched on the northeastern coast of Spain along the Mediterranean Sea, is the vibrant capital of Catalonia. Founded as a Roman colony, it later became the seat of the Crown of Aragon, a medieval power that shaped much of Mediterranean history. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic charm and modern flair: you can wander the winding lanes of the Gothic Quarter, admire Antoni Gaudí’s surreal architecture such as the still-unfinished Sagrada Família, and relax on sandy beaches while cafés serve tapas and cava. Its lively streets, sea breezes and cultural festivals make it a memorable stop for any traveller.

bel.name: Belfast
bel.text: Belfast, the capital of Northern Ireland, sits on the River Lagan where it meets Belfast Lough on the island’s eastern coast. Historically it was the world’s leading ship-building hub, most famously launching the RMS Titanic in 1912. Today the city blends its industrial heritage with a vibrant cultural scene: you can wander the revitalised waterfront, explore museums that recount its past, and enjoy lively pubs, restaurants and street art in the Cathedral Quarter. Friendly locals, green parks and stunning coastal views make Belfast a welcoming place to discover.

ber.name: Berlin
ber.text: Berlin, the vibrant capital of Germany, lies in the northeastern part of the country on the River Spree and is surrounded by the state of Brandenburg. Founded in the 13th century, it became the capital of the Kingdom of Prussia and later the seat of the German Empire, and its historic Brandenburg Gate still marks the former divide between East and West during the Cold War. Today the city buzzes with a mix of modern architecture, world-class museums and leafy parks; cyclists glide along bustling streets, cafés spill onto cobblestones, and the nightlife hums long after the sun sets, making Berlin a lively playground for history lovers and creative explorers alike.

bfn.name: Bloemfontein
bfn.text: Bloemfontein, the judicial capital of South Africa and the heart of the Free State province, began as a British outpost in 1846 and soon became the capital of the Orange Free State republic in 1854. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively university atmosphere, boasting the University of the Free State, the National Museum and the famous rose gardens that give it the nickname “City of Roses”. Its wide avenues, bustling markets and nearby wildlife reserves make it a pleasant base for exploring the central plains and the surrounding Karoo.

bho.name: Bhopal
bho.text: Bhopal, the capital city of Madhya Pradesh in central India, sits on the fertile banks of the Upper Lake and Lower Lake, giving it the nickname “City of Lakes”. It was founded in the early 18th century by the Afghan ruler Dost Mohammad Khan, who established the princely state of Bhopal that later became known for its progressive female rulers in the 20th century. Today the city blends historic charm with modern bustle: you can wander through the elegant Taj-ul-Masjid, explore the well-preserved Bhimbetka rock-shelter caves nearby, and relax by the tranquil lakeside promenades, all while enjoying lively markets, tasty street food and a welcoming atmosphere.

bil.name: Bilbao
bil.text: Bilbao sits on the north-eastern edge of Spain, tucked against the mouth of the Nervión River in the Basque Country and framed by the rolling green hills of the Cantabrian Mountains. The city grew from a medieval trading port and, after the 19th-century industrial boom, became a major centre for steel and shipbuilding. Today, Bilbao is a vibrant mix of old and new: you can stroll along the historic Casco Viejo with its narrow streets and lively pintxos bars, then marvel at the gleaming titanium curves of the Guggenheim Museum, while the riverfront promenades and lush parks offer relaxed, modern ambience perfect for a day of exploration.

bir.name: Birmingham
bir.text: Birmingham sits in the West Midlands of England, about 100 miles north-west of London and 20 miles east of the Welsh border, straddling the River Rea. It grew from a medieval market town into the world’s first industrial city, its factories and canals playing a key role in the Industrial Revolution. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant mix of cultures, from the bustling Bullring shopping centre to the striking modern architecture of the Library of Birmingham, while its historic Jewellery Quarter and lively canalside pubs remind visitors of its rich past.

bjr.name: Bahir Dar
bjr.text: Bahir Dar, perched on the southern shore of Lake Tana in north-west Ethiopia, serves as the capital of the Amhara Region and lies only a short drive from the spectacular Blue Nile Falls. The town grew in importance in the 19th century when it was made the administrative centre of the former Begemder province, and its lakeside promenade is now lined with cafés, hotels and colourful market stalls. Visitors can cruise among the lake’s many islands, explore ancient monasteries accessible only by boat, and enjoy the gentle buzz of daily life against a backdrop of papyrus reeds and bird-song.

bkv.name: Bukavu
bkv.text: Bukavu sits on the southwestern shore of Lake Kivu in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, right on the border with Rwanda and a short drive from the Virunga volcanic range. The town was established by the Belgians in the early twentieth-century as Costermansville and was renamed Bukavu after independence, later becoming the capital of South Kivu province. Today visitors find a laid-back lakeside town with colourful markets, friendly cafés and easy access to boat trips on the lake, as well as hiking routes that lead into the surrounding mountains and the nearby national park.

bna.name: Nashville
bna.text: Nashville, the capital of Tennessee, sits in the heart of the state on the banks of the Cumberland River. The city grew from a frontier settlement founded in 1779 and became the state capital in 1826, later earning its reputation as “Music City” thanks to the establishment of the Grand Ole Opry in 1925 and a thriving recording industry. Today visitors find a lively mix of honky-tonk bars on Broadway, world-class museums such as the Country Music Hall of Fame, and a buzzing food scene ranging from Southern barbecue to inventive farm-to-table eateries, all set against a backdrop of leafy parks and riverfront walkways.

bnn.name: Benin City
bnn.text: Benin City, nestled in southern Nigeria along the meandering banks of the Owan and Edo rivers, sits at the heart of the vibrant Edo State. Founded over a thousand years ago, it was once the capital of the mighty Benin Kingdom, famed for its bronze artistry, massive walls, and sophisticated governance. Today, the city blends that regal legacy with modern hustle: bustling markets, lively festivals, and a growing tech scene. Visitors can explore historic royal palaces, admire intricate ivory and bronze works, and savor delicious local cuisine—all while experiencing the warm hospitality that makes Benin City a living bridge between past and present.

bor.name: Bordeaux
bor.text: Bordeaux, nestled on the banks of the Garonne in southwestern France, lies about 500 km south-west of Paris and is the capital of the Nouvelle-Atlantique region. Founded as a Roman settlement called Burdigala, the city flourished as a major trading port in the 18th century, its wealth famously displayed in the elegant stone façades of the historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Today visitors can wander the wide riverfront promenades, explore the lively markets of the Chartrons district, and sip world-renowned wines in cosy cafés while the modern tram system glides past centuries-old architecture, offering a seamless blend of past and present.

bru.name: Brussels
bru.text: Brussels, the capital of Belgium and the de facto capital of the European Union, sits in the centre of the country where the River Senne meets the countryside of Flanders and Wallonia. First mentioned in the 10th-century records as a modest market town, it grew around the 13th-century Grand-Place, a UNESCO World Heritage site renowned for its ornate guildhalls and the stunning Town Hall. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic charm and modern cosmopolitan life: you can savour world-famous chocolates and waffles, wander past impressive Art Nouveau façades, and soak up the lively atmosphere of cafés and multilingual crowds beneath a sky often brushed with the gentle hue of a summer sunset.

cal.name: Calais
cal.text: Calais sits on the northern coast of France, directly opposite Dover on the Strait of Dover, where the English Channel narrows to just 34 kilometres. Historically it was the principal continental gateway for England, most famously the departure point for the Allies’ D-Day landings in June 1944. Today the town greets visitors with a bustling waterfront, the striking modern Musee des Beaux-Arts, and the massive Calais Lighthouse offering views of the busy ferry terminals and the rolling white cliffs across the water. A walk along the promenade gives a lively mix of cafés, shops and the salty sea air, making it a pleasant stop for both history lovers and seaside wanderers.

cam.name: Cambridge
cam.text: Cambridge is a historic city in the east of England, set on the River Cam about 50 miles north-north-west of London. It grew around the University of Cambridge, which was founded in 1209 and has produced countless scholars, scientists and writers over the centuries. Today the city is a lively mix of medieval colleges with their iconic courtyards and modern cafés, boutique shops and tech start-ups, earning it the nickname “Silicon Fen”. Visitors can stroll along the picturesque riverside, punt on the Cam, explore museums and enjoy the vibrant cultural scene.

car.name: Cardiff
car.text: Cardiff, the capital city of Wales, sits on the southern coast of the United Kingdom where the River Taff meets the Bristol Channel. It grew around Cardiff Castle, a Norman fortress that was later expanded by the Marquesses of Bute in the 19th century and now houses a museum of the city’s medieval and Victorian past. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively waterfront: you can explore the revitalised Cardiff Bay, enjoy a match at the iconic Principality Stadium, wander the bustling streets of the Castle Quarter, and sample Welsh cuisine in cosy pubs and modern restaurants, all within a welcoming, compact urban setting.

cbq.name: Calabar
cbq.text: Calabar, perched on Nigeria’s southeastern coast where the Cross River meets the Atlantic, blends vibrant culture with lush rainforest scenery. Founded in the 15th century as a major hub for the Efik people, it later thrived as a bustling port during the Atlantic trade era, earning the nickname “Queen of the Niger Delta.” Today, Calabar buzzes with tourism, home to the annual Calabar Carnival, historic museums, and eco‑adventures in nearby national parks. Its friendly streets, colonial architecture, and thriving arts scene make it a gateway to the heart of Nigeria’s heritage and natural beauty.

che.name: Cherbourg
che.text: Cherbourg-en-Normandy sits on the tip of the Cotentin Peninsula in north-western France, overlooking the English Channel and the Bay of the Mont Saint-Michel. Founded in the medieval era, the town gained strategic importance during the Second World War and was a key Allied port after the D-Day landings in 1944. Today visitors stroll along the bustling waterfront, explore the impressive Musée de la Cité de la Mer with its historic submarine, and enjoy fresh seafood in a relaxed harbour atmosphere, while the surrounding cliffs and nearby beaches offer striking coastal scenery.

cle.name: Cleveland
cle.text: Cleveland, Ohio, sits on the southern shore of Lake Erie at the mouth of the Cuyahoga River, about 60 miles west of the Pennsylvania border. It was founded in 1796 and named for General Moses Cleaveland, the surveyor who led the expedition that established the settlement. Today the city blends its industrial heritage with a lively cultural scene: the waterfront boasts the iconic Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the bustling West Side Market offers local produce and ethnic foods, and a revitalised downtown brims with museums, theatres and cafés, making a visit both nostalgic and fresh.

clt.name: Charlotte
clt.text: Charlotte, North Carolina, sits in the heart of the American South at the confluence of the Catawba River and Lake Norman, roughly a three-hour drive east of the Appalachian foothills. Founded in 1768 and named for Queen Charlotte, the city grew around a thriving railway hub and later became a centre of the textile industry. Today it buzzes with a mix of sleek skyscrapers and leafy neighbourhoods, offering a lively food scene, museums such as the Levine Center for the Arts, and easy access to outdoor pursuits in the nearby Piedmont countryside, making it a welcoming stop for any traveller.

cok.name: Kochi
cok.text: Kochi, a bustling coastal city in the southwestern Indian state of Kerala, sits on a network of islands and the Arabian Sea, where the historic harbour still echoes its centuries-old role in the spice trade. The Portuguese were the first Europeans to establish a fort here in 1503, later succeeded by the Dutch and the British, leaving a mix of colonial architecture and temples that line the streets of Fort Kochi. Today the city blends the old and the new: you can wander past the iconic Chinese fishing nets, sip coffee in chic cafés, explore lively markets and cruise the serene backwaters, all beneath a warm, tropical climate.

col.name: Cologne
col.text: Cologne lies on the banks of the River Rhine in western Germany, about 70 kilometres north of the Luxembourg border. Founded by the Romans as Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium in the first century AD, it became a major medieval trading hub and the seat of one of the oldest archbishoprics in Europe. Today the city is a lively mix of history and modernity: you can wander beneath the towering spire of the Gothic Cologne Cathedral, explore quirky museums such as the Chocolate Museum, and relax on bustling riverfront terraces while sipping a Kölsch in a traditional brewpub.

cor.name: Cork
cor.text: Cork, situated on the south-west coast of Ireland where the River Lee widens into a bustling harbour, is the country’s second-largest city and a historic trading port that received its charter from King John in 1185. Its medieval streets still echo with the past, while today the city hums with a lively arts scene, cosy cafés and vibrant markets such as the English Market, where you can sample fresh seafood and locally produced cheese. Friendly locals are happy to point you towards colourful pubs, scenic walks along the riverbanks and the striking St Finbarr’s Cathedral, making a visit both charming and contemporary.

csx.name: Changsha
csx.text: Changsha, the capital of Hunan province in south-central China, sits on the banks of the Xiang River about 300 km south of Wuhan. It was the base of the early 20th-century revolutionary leader Mao Zedong, who organised the famous Autumn Harvest Uprising there in 1927. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with lively historic streets: you can wander the bustling Huangxing Road shopping district, savour spicy Hunan cuisine at night markets, and take a leisurely stroll through the ancient Yuelu Academy and its leafy hill, while the riverfront promenade offers views of illuminated bridges and a vibrant river-cruise scene.

cwb.name: Curitiba
cwb.text: Curitiba, the capital of the Brazilian state of Paraná, lies in the south-central part of the country about 400 km west of the coastal city of Florianópolis. The town began as a modest settlement in 1693 and was designated the state capital in 1853, later becoming renowned for its pioneering urban planning and extensive green spaces. Today visitors find a clean, well-organised city with an efficient bus network, striking modernist architecture, and a network of parks and tree-lined avenues; highlights include the glass-capped Botanical Garden, the bustling farmers’ market at Rua das Flores, and a vibrant culinary scene that blends traditional Brazilian flavours with European influences.

die.name: Dieppe
die.text: Dieppe is a charming coastal town in the Normandy region of north-western France, set on the English Channel about 170 km north of Paris. It grew famous in 1942 when Allied forces launched a daring raid on its harbour, an event that helped shape the later D-Day landings. Today the town is a relaxed seaside destination with a bustling fishing port, a long pebble beach perfect for strolling, and a lively promenade lined with cafés and shops. Visitors can wander the historic Château de Dieppe, explore maritime museums, and enjoy fresh seafood while watching the Atlantic breeze roll in.

dov.name: Dover
dov.text: Dover sits on the southeastern tip of England, facing the narrow Strait of Dover that separates Britain from France, and its white chalk cliffs dominate the coastline. The town has been a key gateway for centuries; Roman and later medieval forts were built here, and the famous Dover Castle has guarded the coast since the 12th century. Today the promenade is bustling with cafés, souvenir stalls and the iconic white-cliff walk, while ferries whisk visitors across to Calais in under two hours. With its dramatic sea views, historic sites and lively harbour, Dover feels both a living port and a reminder of Britain’s maritime heritage.

dtt.name: Detroit
dtt.text: Detroit, Michigan, lies on the banks of the Detroit River directly opposite Windsor, Ontario, in the heart of the American Midwest. The city earned its fame as the cradle of the automobile industry, with Henry Ford establishing the Ford Motor Company in 1903 and introducing the moving assembly line a decade later. Today, visitors find a vibrant mix of historic art deco theatres, bustling street art districts and revitalised waterfront parks, while the legacy of motor-car manufacturing is celebrated in museums such as the Henry Ford and the Detroit Institute of Arts, offering a lively blend of culture and innovation.

dub.name: Dublin
dub.text: Dublin, the capital of Ireland, sits on the east coast where the River Liffey meets the Irish Sea, spreading over the low-lying plains of the province of Leinster. Founded by the Vikings in the 9th century, it later became the seat of English rule and the birthplace of many literary giants, including James Joyce. Today the city buzzes with a warm, welcoming atmosphere: you can wander past Georgian townhouses, sip a coffee in a bustling café, explore lively markets, and enjoy traditional music spilling from cosy pubs, all while the modern skyline rises behind the historic streets.

dzo.name: Mayotte (Dzaoudzi)
dzo.text: Mayotte (Dzaoudzi) – a tiny jewel nestled in the heart of the Indian Ocean, just north of Madagascar and off the coast of Mozambique. Once a strategic stop for Arab traders and later a French colony in the 19th century, it became an overseas department of France in 2011, blending African, Malagasy and European influences. Today, Dzaoudzi, the former capital, welcomes visitors with turquoise lagoons, lush volcanic hills and a vibrant Creole culture. From bustling markets to pristine marine parks, Mayotte offers a unique glimpse of French‑administered paradise where tradition meets modernity on every sun‑kissed shore.

edi.name: Edinburgh
edi.text: Edinburgh, perched on the east coast of Scotland where the River Forth meets the North Sea, is a compact city of striking contrasts. Its most famous historic landmark, the medieval castle that dominates the skyline, has guarded the city since the 12th century and was the site where the Scottish Crown Jewels are kept. Today the streets are alive with a mix of cobbled Old Town alleys and sleek New Town squares, bustling cafés, and world-class museums; the annual festivals fill the air with music, theatre and a lively, welcoming buzz for visitors of all ages.

enu.name: Enugu
enu.text: Enugu, the “Coal City” of Nigeria, sits in the verdant hills of the southeast, perched at an altitude of 590 metres on the edge of the Udi Plateau. Founded in the early 1900s after rich coal seams were discovered, it quickly grew into a colonial mining hub and later became the capital of the former Eastern Region. Today, Enugu blends its storied past with vibrant urban energy—home to bustling markets, thriving universities, and a blossoming tech scene. Its warm hospitality, lively music, and lush gardens make it a gateway to Igbo culture and a rising centre of commerce in Nigeria.

fbm.name: Kisangani
fbm.text: Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo Province in the north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, lies on the banks of the mighty Congo River where it meets the Lualaba tributary. Founded in the late 19th century as a trading post for the Belgian Congo, it later became an important military base during the Congo Crisis of the 1960s. Today the town offers a relaxed riverside atmosphere, with colourful markets selling fresh fish and local crafts, boat trips that showcase the impressive rapids of the Congo, and easy access to nearby rain-forest trails for adventurous visitors.

fln.name: Florianopolis
fln.text: Florianópolis, the capital of Brazil’s southern state of Santa Catarina, sits on the island of Santa Catarina and a thin strip of the mainland opposite the mainland city of São José. The town was founded by the Portuguese in 1673 as Nossa Senhora do Desterro and later renamed after the explorer Floriano Pereira. Today the city is a laid-back seaside haven, famed for its more than forty beaches that range from lively surf spots to tranquil coves, a bustling market of fresh seafood, colourful colonial streets and a vibrant nightlife that spills onto the sand at sunset.

fnc.name: Funchal
fnc.text: Funchal—nestled on the sun‑kissed southern coast of Portugal’s Madeira Island, this vibrant capital greets you with a tapestry of cliffs, turquoise bays and fragrant gardens. Founded in the early 15th century by Portuguese explorers, it grew from a modest fishing village into a crucial Atlantic hub for sugar, wine and later tourism. Today, Funchal dazzles visitors with its historic cobblestone streets, colorful market stalls, and a lively waterfront lined with cafés, museums and the famed cable‑car that climbs to Monte’s lush terraces. It’s a blend of old‑world charm and modern island energy—perfect for the curious traveler.

fra.name: Frankfurt
fra.text: Frankfurt, situated on the River Main in the state of Hesse in central Germany, is a bustling financial hub often nicknamed “Mainhattan” for its skyline of glass-clad towers. Historically it was the site of the first Frankfurt Parliament in 1848, Germany’s first freely elected national assembly. Today the city blends modernity with charm: you can wander the historic Römer square, explore museums along the Museumsufer, and enjoy the fragrant apple-wine taverns of the Alt-Sachsenhausen district, all while the lively streets buzz with shoppers, commuters and international visitors.

ftz.name: Fortaleza
ftz.text: Fortaleza, the bustling coastal capital of Brazil’s Ceará state, sits on a wide, sandy bay on the Atlantic Ocean. Founded in the early 17th century as a Portuguese fort to protect the region from French incursions, the city still bears the imprint of its colonial past in the historic centre and the nearby Forte de Nossa Senhora da Assunção. Today visitors are greeted by a lively promenade lined with palm-fringed beaches, vibrant markets selling tropical fruit and handcrafted jewellery, and a thriving nightlife that spills from beach bars into colourful street festivals, all under a warm, sunny sky.

gau.name: Guwahati
gau.text: Guwahati, the bustling gateway to Northeast India, sits on the south bank of the Brahmaputra River in the state of Assam. It grew around the ancient Kamakhya Temple, a revered Shakti shrine that has attracted pilgrims for centuries and was mentioned in early medieval texts. Today the city blends modern cafés, colourful markets and leafy riverfront promenades, offering river cruises, wildlife parks and easy trips to nearby tea-plantation hills. Visitors enjoy the lively blend of Assamese culture, the aroma of fresh tea, and the backdrop of mist-shrouded hills rising beyond the flowing Brahmaputra.

gla.name: Glasgow
gla.text: Glasgow sits on the River Clyde in western Scotland, about 45 miles northwest of Edinburgh and a short train ride from the Irish Sea coast. Once a booming hub of shipbuilding and industry in the 19th century, the city’s historic legacy is visible in its grand Victorian architecture and the famous Riverside Museum, which celebrates its maritime past. Today Glasgow thrives as a vibrant cultural centre, famous for its lively music scene, world-class galleries such as the Gallery of Modern Art, and a friendly, laid-back atmosphere that welcomes visitors to explore its bustling cafés, leafy parks and striking street art.

goi.name: Goiania
goi.text: Goiania, the vibrant capital of the Brazilian state of Goiás, lies in the heart of the country’s interior, about 200 km south-west of Brasília. Planned from scratch in the early 1930s, it officially became the state capital in 1937, replacing the historic town of Goiás Velho and sparking rapid growth. Today the city dazzles visitors with its wide, tree-lined avenues, striking modernist buildings such as the colourful Praça Cívica designed by Oscar Niemeyer, and a lively cultural scene that includes bustling markets, lively cafés and the nearby Parque Vaca Brava, a favourite spot for picnics and bird-watching.

gra.name: Granada
gra.text: Granada, nestled at the foot of the Sierra Nevada in southern Spain, straddles the fertile plains where the Darro and Genil rivers converge. Founded by the Romans and later transformed by Visigoths, Moors, and Christians, this city bears layers of history—from its ancient Albaicín quarters to the iconic Alhambra, a UNESCO masterpiece of Islamic art. Today, Granada pulses with youthful energy thanks to its bustling university, vibrant tapas scene, and year‑round festivals that blend tradition and modern flair. As you wander its cobbled streets, you’ll feel the timeless dialogue between past and present that makes Granada a true cultural crossroads.

gur.name: Guiria
gur.text: Guiria sits on the Caribbean coast of eastern Venezuela, the capital of Valdez Municipality in Sucre state. Founded in the mid-eighteenth century, it soon became a vital cacao-export port and later served as a naval point during the Venezuelan War of Independence. Today the town is a colourful blend of colonial houses, lively markets and a promenade lined with fresh-seafood stalls, while its beaches attract both locals and visitors seeking sun and gentle surf. The warm, relaxed atmosphere reflects its fishing heritage and growing tourism.

har.name: Harwich
har.text: Harwich is a bustling little port town in the county of Essex, perched on the estuary where the River Stour meets the North Sea, just a short train ride from London. Historically it was an important naval base and commercial harbour, with the Harwich Redoubt built in the early 1800s to protect the coast during the Napoleonic wars. Today the town feels relaxed yet lively: you can stroll along the historic waterfront, watch ferries set out for the Netherlands and Denmark, explore the maritime museum, and enjoy fresh seafood in cosy cafés while the sea breeze carries the scent of sails and salt.

het.name: Hohhot
het.text: Hohhot, the capital of Inner Mongolia in northern China, sits on the gentle slopes of the Yulong Grasslands about 150 km south of the Great Wall’s Badaling section. Historically it was a key trading hub on the ancient caravan routes between China and Mongolia, flourishing under the Qing dynasty when it became the regional administrative centre. Today the city blends wide boulevards with traditional Mongolian yurts, offering bustling markets where you can sample roasted lamb and milk tea, modern museums that showcase nomadic culture, and leafy parks perfect for a leisurely stroll.

hgh.name: Hangzhou
hgh.text: Hangzhou, a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, lies on the banks of the Qiantang River at the foot of the famous West Lake. It has been celebrated since the Tang dynasty as a capital of the Southern Song, when emperors built the picturesque gardens and temples that still inspire poets today. Modern visitors find a blend of ancient charm and sleek development: you can stroll among lotus-filled waters, sip longjing tea in historic teahouses, and then hop on a high-speed train or explore vibrant tech parks and bustling night markets, all within a city famed for its natural beauty and hospitality.

hly.name: Holyhead
hly.text: Holyhead sits on the western tip of Holy Island, off the coast of Anglesey in North Wales, and serves as the United Kingdom’s busiest ferry gateway to Dublin. The town grew around a Roman fort known as Caer y Ffos, evidence of its strategic importance for centuries, and later expanded with the 19th-century Admiralty Pier that still frames the harbour. Today Holyhead blends a bustling port atmosphere with rugged coastal scenery: you can stroll along the promenade, watch ferries swing in and out, explore the maritime museum, and enjoy fresh seafood while the sea breezes carry the scent of salt and history.

hmn.name: Hamilton, Bermuda
hmn.text: Hamilton, the capital of Bermuda, sits on the island’s central south coast overlooking Hamilton Harbour. Laid out in 1790 and named for Governor Sir Henry Hamilton, it quickly became the island’s administrative centre, replacing the older capital at St George’s. Landmarks such as the mid-nineteenth-century Cathedral of the Most Holy Trinity and the Bermuda National Museum echo its maritime and colonial past. Today the city blends pastel-coloured storefronts, a bustling harbour filled with cruise ships, and a thriving financial district, offering visitors a lively mix of heritage and modern island life.

hoh.name: Hook of Holland
hoh.text: Hook of Holland is a seaside town at the western tip of South Holland, where the Nieuwe Waterweg canal meets the North Sea, just a short drive west of Rotterdam. It was the departure point for the first regular passenger ferry service to Harwich, England, which began in 1893 and helped cement its role as a gateway between the Netherlands and Britain. Today the promenade is lined with colourful beach huts, modern cafés and a bustling ferry terminal, while the wide sandy beach and the iconic windmills on the dunes offer relaxed strolls and striking sunset views over the busy shipping lane.

hrg.name: Hurghada
hrg.text: Hurghada is a bustling seaside town on Egypt’s Red Sea coast, about 500 km southeast of Cairo. Originally a small fishing village, it grew rapidly after the 1970s when the government promoted tourism along the Red Sea, and today it is a major gateway for diving and beach holidays. The town’s promenade is lined with cafés, souvenir stalls and modern hotels, while the crystal-clear waters host vibrant coral reefs teeming with marine life. Visitors can spend the day lounging on golden sands, exploring nearby desert dunes on a quad bike, or hopping on a boat to snorkel among colourful fish and ancient shipwrecks.

ibd.name: Ibadan
ibd.text: Ibadan, the bustling heart of southwestern Nigeria, sits on a gentle plateau between the Ogun and Oyo rivers, just a short drive north of Lagos. Founded in the 1820s as a war‑camp for the Yoruba, it grew into a thriving commercial hub and the historic seat of the powerful Ibadan Kingdom. Today, the city blends old‑world charm—think colonial‑era architecture and the famous Cocoa House—with modern universities, tech startups, and a vibrant arts scene. From bustling markets to leafy university campuses, Ibadan remains a cultural crossroads, showcasing Nigeria’s rich heritage while forging a dynamic future.

ind.name: Indianapolis
ind.text: Indianapolis sits in the heart of Indiana, midway between Chicago and Cincinnati, and serves as the state’s capital and largest city. Established in 1821 as a planned centre for the new state, it quickly grew around the crossroads of the National Road and the Wabash and Erie Canal. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with wide, tree-lined streets and a vibrant cultural scene; visitors can stroll along the Canal Walk, explore the expansive Indianapolis Museum of Art, and feel the buzz of the famous motor-sport atmosphere at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, all within a friendly, Midwestern setting.

ixc.name: Chandigarh
ixc.text: Chandigarh, perched at the foothills of the Shivalik range in north-western India, is the joint capital of the states of Punjab and Haryana. Designed by the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier after India’s independence, it was one of the first planned cities in the country and was formally inaugurated in 1966. Today the city feels spacious and modern, with tree-lined avenues, wide boulevards and striking concrete buildings punctuated by colourful gardens. Visitors can stroll through the beautifully laid-out Rock Garden, relax by Sukhna Lake, or sip tea at a bustling café while watching locals go about their day.

jos.name: Jos
jos.text: Jos, perched on the Jos Plateau in the heart of Nigeria’s middle belt, sits at about 1,200 metres above sea-level, giving it a noticeably cooler climate than much of the country. The town grew in the early 1900s as a British colonial hill station and soon became the centre of the country’s tin-mining boom, a legacy still hinted at in the old mines and the colourful displays at the National Museum. Today visitors find a pleasant mix of bustling markets, craft shops and relaxed cafés, with easy trips to nearby wildlife parks and scenic high-land walks that showcase the region’s distinctive pine-covered hills.

kgf.name: Karaganda
kgf.text: Karaganda, a city in central Kazakhstan, lies on the steppe about 230 kilometres south-east of the capital Astana. It grew rapidly in the 1930s when Soviet authorities developed large coal mines in the region, turning the former settlement into an industrial centre. Today the city offers a mix of Soviet-era architecture and modern amenities: visitors can explore the striking Karaganda Regional Museum, stroll along the wide avenues lined with statues and fountains, and enjoy the nearby parklands that provide a pleasant contrast to the surrounding flat landscape. The friendly locals and hearty Kazakh cuisine make a stop here a memorable part of any Central Asian itinerary.

kmn.name: Kerman
kmn.text: Kerman, a sprawling city in south-central Iran, sits at the foot of the Zagros mountains about 1,600 km southeast of Tehran. It has long been a key stop on historic trade routes, famously serving as a caravan hub for the Silk Road and home to the 12th-century Jameh Mosque, one of the region’s oldest surviving religious sites. Today the city blends ancient charm with modern bustle: narrow bazaars spill colourful spices and pistachios, rooftop cafés offer views of the stark desert beyond, and the nearby Lut Desert, a UNESCO World Heritage site, draws adventurers seeking surreal, sun-scorched landscapes.

kuf.name: Samara
kuf.text: Samara, Russia, sits on the right bank of the Volga River where it meets the Samara River, about 900 km southeast of Moscow. Founded in the late 16th century, the city grew into a key ship-building centre and later became an important industrial hub during the Soviet era. Today it feels spacious and modern, with wide boulevards lined by leafy parks and striking Soviet-era architecture alongside trendy cafés and riverfront promenades. Visitors can stroll along the embankment for panoramic views of the Volga, explore the lively waterfront market, and enjoy the blend of historic museums and vibrant cultural life that gives Samara its friendly, contemporary vibe.

lhw.name: Lanzhou
lhw.text: Lanzhou, the capital of Gansu Province in north-western China, sits on the banks of the mighty Yellow River where the Loess Plateau meets the desert fringe. Founded over two thousand years ago, it became a key hub on the ancient Silk Road, linking Chinese heartlands with Central Asia. Today the city blends modern high-rise towers with bustling night markets; you can sip freshly-made Lanzhou beef noodle soup beside the river promenade, explore the colourful Zhongshan Bridge, or take a short bus ride to the striking Bingling Grottoes perched on the cliffs of the nearby Liujiaxia Reservoir. The mix of history, culture and striking scenery makes a visit both lively and memorable.

lil.name: Lille
lil.text: Lille sits in the far north of France, just a short train ride from the Belgian border and a stone’s throw from the coast of the North Sea. Founded as a Roman settlement, it later became the capital of French Flanders and was a key stronghold during the Wars of Religion, when the city’s famous citadel was constructed by Vauban in the 17th century. Today Lille buzzes with a lively mix of historic cobbled streets, sleek modern boutiques and bustling markets; its cafés spill onto the Grand Place, and the vibrant cultural scene – from museums to street art – makes wandering its neighbourhoods a delight for any traveller.

liv.name: Liverpool
liv.text: Liverpool sits on the western edge of the Mersey Estuary in north-west England, its waterfront stretching along the River Mersey. Historically it grew into a major global port in the 18th and 19th centuries, famously serving as the gateway for many emigrants to the New World and for the trans-Atlantic trade that shaped the city’s wealth. Today the city buzzes with music, sport and culture: you can wander the historic Albert Dock, admire the impressive waterfront UNESCO World Heritage sites, enjoy lively pubs and cafés, and catch the vibrant street art and festivals that give Liverpool its warm, welcoming character.

lko.name: Lucknow
lko.text: Lucknow, the capital city of Uttar Pra Pradesh in northern India, rests on the banks of the gently flowing Gomti River and lies about 500 kilometres east of New Delhi. Historically it was the centre of the 1857 Indian Rebellion and later became renowned for its Nawabi culture, evident in the elegant architecture of the Bara Imambara and the bustling markets of Aminabad. Today, visitors find a lively mix of old and new: colonial-era streets lined with chic cafés, fragrant street-food stalls serving kebabs and biryani, and tranquil gardens where you can watch locals go about their day against a backdrop of grand monuments and modern malls.

lon.name: London
lon.text: London, the capital of the United Kingdom, sits on the River Thames in southeastern England, straddling both banks of the waterway. Founded by the Romans as Londinium around AD 43, the city grew into a bustling medieval port and later the heart of the British Empire. Today, London feels like a vibrant mosaic of history and modernity: you can stand beneath the towering glass of the Shard, wander the historic cobbles of Covent Garden, and hear the chime of Big Ben while sipping a coffee in a bustling café. Museums, parks, theatres and diverse neighbourhoods make every visit feel fresh and exciting.

lpg.name: Las Palmas
lpg.text: Las Palmas, the sun‑kissed capital of Gran Canaria, sits on the island’s northeastern coast where the Atlantic meets volcanic hills and golden beaches. Founded in 1478 by Spanish conquistadors as “Real Villa de La Luz,” the city grew from a modest fishing port into a bustling entrepôt, its historic Vegueta district preserving cobblestone streets and Moorish‑influenced architecture. Today, Las Palmas is a vibrant cultural hub—home to lively markets, world‑class museums, and the famed Las Canteras promenade—while serving as a modern gateway for tourism, commerce, and renewable‑energy innovation across the Canary archipelago. Join us as we explore its timeless charm and forward‑looking spirit.

lyo.name: Lyon
lyo.text: Lyon, nestled at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône rivers in east-central France, is the country’s third-largest city and a historic crossroads of trade. Founded by the Romans as Lugdunum in 43 BC, it later became a key centre of the silk industry in the 19th century, a heritage still visible in its traboules—hidden passageways linking the old neighbourhoods. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant culinary scene, from bustling bouchons serving traditional Lyonnaise dishes to Michelin-starred restaurants, while its UNESCO-listed old town offers cobbled streets, Renaissance architecture and stunning views from the hilltop Basilica of Notre-Dam de Fourvière.

mad.name: Madrid
mad.text: Madrid, the vibrant capital of Spain, sits in the heart of the Iberian Peninsula on the Manzanares River, surrounded by the rolling Castilian plains. Founded as a modest fortress in the ninth-century, it became the royal seat when King Philip II moved his court there in 1561, establishing the city as the centre of the Spanish Empire. Today the city buzzes with a mix of historic grandeur and modern energy: you can stroll through the leafy Retiro Park, admire world-class art in the Prado, savour tapas in lively plazas, and feel the warm, cosmopolitan rhythm that makes Madrid a favourite stop for travellers.

man.name: Manchester
man.text: Manchester, nestled in the north-west of England on the River Irwell, grew from a modest medieval market town into a powerhouse of the Industrial Revolution, famously pioneering cotton spinning and railway engineering in the 19th century. Today the city buzzes with a vibrant mix of culture and sport: you can explore world-class museums such as the Science and Industry Museum, savour street food in the bustling Curry Mile, and feel the electric atmosphere of a match at the iconic Old Trafford. Its leafy canals, modern architecture and lively music scene make Manchester a friendly, energetic stop for any traveller.

mar.name: Marseille
mar.text: Marseille, perched on the southeastern coast of France where the Mediterranean meets the Rhône-Alpes region, is France’s oldest city, founded by Greek sailors from Phocaea around 600 BC. Its historic Vieux-Port still bustles with fishing boats and cafés, while the striking basilica of Notre-Dame de la Garde watches over the harbor from its hilltop perch. Today the city mixes vibrant street art, lively markets selling olives and bouillabaisse, and a lively waterfront promenade that leads to modern museums and sandy beaches. The blend of ancient stone streets, multicultural flavours and stunning sea views makes a visit feel both timeless and refreshingly contemporary.

mbm.name: Mbuji-Mayi
mbm.text: Mbuji-Mayi, the capital of Kasai-Oriental province in the heart of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, lies on the Sankuru River about 300 km south-west of the national capital Kinshasa. Formerly called Bakwanga, the town grew rapidly after independence because it sits above one of the world’s richest diamond deposits and became the centre of the state-run Société Minière de Bakwanga. Today visitors find a city of wide avenues and colourful markets where traders sell fresh produce, fabrics and locally-cut diamonds; the pace is relaxed, the streets are lined with modest shops and cafés, and the surrounding countryside offers chances to see traditional Kasai villages and the rolling savannah beyond.

mci.name: Kansas City
mci.text: Kansas City, straddling the border between Missouri and Kansas in the American Midwest, sits on the confluence of the Missouri and Kansas rivers. Founded in the early 19th century, the city grew around the historic Santa Fe Trail, which made it a key gateway for westward expansion. Today visitors enjoy a vibrant mix of jazz clubs, world-class barbecue joints and impressive art installations such as the towering “Lion” sculpture in the downtown plaza. The River Market district offers bustling farmers’ markets and historic warehouses converted into cafés, while the nearby Country Club Plaza delights shoppers with its Spanish-style architecture and lively street ambience.

mco.name: Orlando
mco.text: Orlando lies in the heart of central Florida, roughly midway between the Atlantic coast and the Gulf of Mexico and about an hour’s drive north of the bustling city of Tampa. Founded in the late 19th century, the town grew around the citrus industry and was officially incorporated in 1875; its name honours a soldier who fought in the Second Seminole War. Today the city is synonymous with world-class theme parks such as Walt Disney World and Universal Studios, but it also offers vibrant dining precincts, leafy lakeside parks and a lively arts scene, making it a colourful and welcoming destination for visitors of all ages.

mem.name: Memphis
mem.text: Memphis, Tennessee, lies on the mighty Mississippi River in the southwestern corner of the state, bordering Arkansas. Founded in 1819 and named after the ancient Egyptian city, it quickly became a crucial river port and a crossroads of American culture. Today the city buzzes with the legacy of blues and rock ’n’ roll: you can stroll down historic Beale Street, visit the iconic Graceland home of Elvis Presley, and explore the National Civil Rights Museum at the former Lorraine Motel. With its lively music venues, riverfront parks and famous barbecue, Memphis feels both steeped in history and unmistakably vibrant.

mmk.name: Murmansk
mmk.text: Murmansk sits on the Kola Bay at the entrance to the Barents Sea, far above the Arctic Circle on Russia’s north-western coast. Founded in 1916 as a supply port for the war effort, it became the only ice-free harbour in the Soviet north, playing a crucial role in both World Wars and the Cold War naval fleet. Today the city greets visitors with colourful wooden houses, a bustling waterfront promenade, and the striking Alyosha monument overlooking the sea. In summer the midnight sun brightens the streets, while winter offers chances to see the Northern Lights and sample hearty Arctic cuisine in cosy cafés.

mqx.name: Mekelle
mqx.text: Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia’s Tigray Region, lies on the high plateau of northern Ethiopia at about 2,500 metres above sea level, roughly 780 km north-north-east of Addis Ababa. Historically it was the seat of Emperor Yohannes IV, who ruled the country from the late 19th century until his death in 1889, and it later became an important administrative centre during the Imperial era. Today the city offers a lively market where traders display woven textiles, spices and coffee

msp.name: Minneapolis
msp.text: Minneapolis, a vibrant city in the Upper Midwest of the United States, sits on the banks of the Mississippi River where it meets the scenic Chain of Lakes. Founded in the 1850s, it grew rapidly as a centre for flour milling, once boasting the world’s largest grain processing capacity and earning the nickname “Mill City.” Today visitors enjoy a blend of modern art, bustling food markets and extensive parkland: the Walker Art Center and its iconic Spoonbridge sculpture, the lively North Loop eateries, and miles of bike-friendly trails that wind through lush lakes and riverfront promenades, offering a fresh, lively urban experience.

mta.name: Matadi
mta.text: Matadi, a bustling port town on the western edge of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sits at the mouth of the Congo River about 150 km from Kinshasa and just a short distance from the Atlantic coast. Founded in the early 1880s as a key terminus for the railway that linked the interior to the sea, it grew into the country’s main gateway for imports and exports. Today visitors find a lively waterfront lined with colourful markets, colonial-era buildings and lively cafés, while the humid climate and constant river traffic give the town a vibrant, slightly chaotic charm that feels both historic and unmistakably modern.

nan.name: Nantes
nan.text: Nantes, situated on the banks of the Loire in western France, is a vibrant city that blends river-side charm with a rich maritime heritage. Once the historic capital of the Duchy of Brittany and a major port for Atlantic trade, its legacy is still visible in the impressive Château des Ducs de Bretagne and the preserved 18th-century shipyards of the Cité des Congrès. Today visitors can wander along the lively quays, explore the whimsical Machines of the Isle of Nantes with its giant mechanical elephant, and enjoy bustling markets, cafés and contemporary art galleries that give the city a lively, modern feel.

nhv.name: Newhaven
nhv.text: Newhaven is a small coastal town in East Sussex, perched on the mouth of the River Ouse where it meets the English Channel, just a short drive east of Brighton. It grew around a medieval fishing harbour that later became an important packet-boat terminal for cross-Channel services in the 19th century, and the town’s historic harbour walls still echo that maritime past. Today visitors can stroll along the lively promenade, watch the ferries to Dieppe, enjoy fresh seafood in cosy pubs, and take in sweeping sea views from the nearby cliffs, all in a relaxed, friendly atmosphere.

nic.name: Nice
nic.text: Nice, perched on the sun-kissed French Riviera between the Mediterranean Sea and the foothills of the Alps, is a vibrant coastal city in the southeast of France. It grew from a small fishing settlement into a fashionable resort after the railway arrived in 1864, attracting artists and aristocrats alike. Today the promenade along the famous Baie des Anges is lined with palm trees, cafés and the iconic pebble beach, while the narrow streets of the old town reveal colourful baroque houses, bustling markets and the scent of socca. Visitors can stroll the promenade, explore museums such as the Musée Matisse, and enjoy the blend of French and Italian influences that give Nice its distinct charm.

nkg.name: Nanjing
nkg.text: Nanjing, situated on the lower reaches of the Yangtze River in eastern China, was the capital of several Chinese dynasties and the seat of the early Republic of China, famously hosting the 1912 provisional government. Today the city blends its deep history with a lively modern vibe: you can wander along the historic city wall, explore the solemn Memorial Hall of the Nanjing Massacre, and then relax in bustling pedestrian streets lined with cafés, boutique shops and neon-lit skyscrapers. The surrounding Qinhuai River area offers charming lantern-lit night walks, while nearby Purple Mountain provides peaceful trails and spectacular views over the urban landscape.

nng.name: Nanning
nng.text: Nanning, the capital of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China, sits on the banks of the Nan River a few hundred kilometres from the Vietnamese border. Historically it served as a regional administrative centre during the Tang dynasty and later became the seat of the provincial government after the establishment of the People’s Republic. Today the city is celebrated for its lush, tree-lined streets and plentiful parks, earning it the nickname “Green City”. Visitors can wander the lively Qingxiu Mountain, sample the spicy Zhuang cuisine in bustling night markets, and enjoy a relaxed blend of modern malls and traditional riverfront scenery.

npr.name: Napier
npr.text: Napier, perched on the edge of Hawke Bay on New Zealand’s North Island, first grew as a modest 19th-century settlement before a devastating magnitude-7.8 earthquake in 1931 razed much of the town. The rebuilding gave it the world-renowned Art Deco façade that still lines its streets, making it a living museum of the style. Today the city buzzes with cafés, boutique shops and vibrant markets, while its sun-washed beaches and nearby vineyards draw both locals and travellers seeking fine wine, coastal walks and a taste of heritage.

nuk.name: Nukus
nuk.text: Nukus, the capital of Uzbekistan’s autonomous Republic of Karakalpakstan, lies on the banks of the Amu Darya in the far west of the country, close to the Turkmen border and the edge of the Kyzylkum desert. Founded in the late-19th century as a small settlement, it became the regional centre when the Karakalpak Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was created in 1932. Today the town is famous for the Savitsky Museum, which houses one of the world’s largest collections of Soviet-era avant-garde art, and its wide, tree-lined streets provide a surprisingly relaxed base for exploring nearby desert landscapes and the historic fortress of Khiva.

okc.name: Oklahoma City
okc.text: Oklahoma City lies in the heart of the American Midwest, perched on the banks of the North Fork of the Canadian River in the state of Oklahoma. Founded during the Land Run of 1889, the city grew rapidly as a centre for cattle trading and later for oil production, shaping its rugged frontier character. Today it offers a lively blend of modern culture and historic charm: the vibrant Bricktown entertainment district buzzes with restaurants and river-front walks, the impressive National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum showcases Western art, and spacious parks provide a welcoming atmosphere for visitors of all ages.

oma.name: Omaha
oma.text: Omaha, Nebraska, sits on the western bank of the Missouri River at the heart of the Midwestern United States, roughly three-hundred miles north of Kansas City. Founded in 1854 as a frontier outpost, it quickly became a key stop on the Oregon Trail and later the eastern terminus of the first transcontinental railroad, cementing its role in westward expansion. Today the city blends river-front charm with a lively cultural scene: the historic Old Market district offers cobbled streets, independent shops and cafés, while the Henry Doorly Zoo, modern museums and a bustling riverwalk give visitors a pleasant mix of nature, history and contemporary Midwestern hospitality.

oxf.name: Oxford
oxf.text: Oxford, set in the heart of southern England on the River Thames, lies about 60 miles northwest of London. The city grew around the University of Oxford, founded in the 12th century and renowned as the oldest English-speaking university in the world. Today visitors can wander its historic cobbled streets, admire the dreaming spires of colleges such as Christ Church and Magdalen, and enjoy bustling market squares, independent bookshops and riverside punts. With a lively mix of academia, museums and cosy cafés, Oxford feels both timeless and vibrantly modern.

par.name: Paris
par.text: Paris, the capital of France, sits on the banks of the River Seine in the north-central part of the country. Founded by the Celtic Parisii tribe, it became an imperial centre when the Romans built Lutetia on the island now known as Île de la Cité, and it later grew into a hub of art, fashion and cuisine. Today the city dazzles visitors with its iconic skyline of Haussmannian boulevards, world-renowned museums such as the Louvre, and lively cafés spilling onto cobbled streets. A stroll along the Seine offers a mix of historic monuments, modern shops and the unmistakable buzz of a metropolis that still feels romantic and vibrant.

pdl.name: Ponta Delgada
pdl.text: Ponta Delgada – the vibrant capital of Portugal’s Azores archipelago, perched on the southern coast of São Miguel Island.  Nestled in the mid‑Atlantic, this charming town blends volcanic landscapes with sweeping ocean views, a natural gateway between Europe and the Americas.  Founded in the 15th century by Portuguese settlers, it grew from a modest fishing village into a key stopover for trans‑Atlantic whalers and explorers, its historic cobblestone streets still echoing centuries of maritime heritage.  Today, Ponta Delgada thrives as a cultural hub—buzzing cafés, lively festivals, and eco‑tourism adventures—while preserving its rich past amid stunning cliffs, geothermal springs and world‑class cuisine.

pdx.name: Portland
pdx.text: Portland, Oregon, lies in the Pacific Northwest of the United States where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet, about 70 miles east of the Pacific coast. Founded in 1845 and incorporated in 1851, the city grew around timber and river trade and later became known for its progressive urban planning. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of lush parks, bike-friendly streets and a thriving food scene, with famous coffee roasters, food-truck pods and a bustling Saturday market by the waterfront. The surrounding mountains and nearby vineyards add outdoor adventure and wine-tasting to the city’s laid-back, eco-conscious charm.

pee.name: Perm
pee.text: Perm lies on the banks of the wide, winding Kama River at the western foothills of the Ural Mountains, marking the traditional divide between European and Asian Russia. It was founded in 1723 as a modest settlement serving the salt-mining industry and grew into a key industrial hub during the 19th-century railway boom. Today the city offers a lively mix of cultural attractions – the striking Perm Opera and Ballet Theatre, the contemporary art-filled Perm Museum of Contemporary Art, and the open-air Koltushi Park – alongside cosy cafés and bustling markets, making a pleasant base for exploring both river scenery and the surrounding forested hills.

phl.name: Philadelphia
phl.text: Philadelphia, nestled in the southeastern corner of Pennsylvania along the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, is a city steeped in American history; it was the meeting place for the Continental Congress where the Declaration of Independence was debated and the Constitution signed. Today the streets buzz with a lively mix of historic cobblestones and modern skyscrapers, inviting visitors to stroll past the iconic Liberty Bell, explore world-class museums on the “Museum Mile,” and savour diverse food markets ranging from classic cheesesteaks to global street fare, all set against a backdrop of vibrant neighbourhoods and green riverfront parks.

phx.name: Phoenix
phx.text: Phoenix, Arizona, lies in the heart of the Sonoran Desert about 350 miles southeast of Las Vegas and 200 miles north of the Mexican border, cradled by the Salt River and surrounded by low mountains. Founded in 1867 as a farming community near the Hohokam canals, it grew into the capital of the territory and later the state in 1912. Today the city blends modern skyline and sprawling suburbs with desert-cactus scenery, offering vibrant arts districts, world-class museums and easy access to hiking in nearby Camelback Mountain, making it a warm, lively base for exploring the Southwest.

pit.name: Pittsburgh
pit.text: Pittsburgh, situated at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela and Ohio rivers in western Pennsylvania, grew from a frontier fort into a powerhouse of industry in the 19th century, famously known for its steel production that earned the city the nickname “Steel City”. Today the skyline is a blend of historic brick warehouses and sleek glass towers, while the river valleys provide scenic bridges and bustling waterfront parks. Visitors can explore vibrant neighbourhoods such as the Strip District’s food markets, the cultural riches of the Carnegie museums, and enjoy a lively craft-beer scene against a backdrop of rolling hills.

ply.name: Plymouth
ply.text: Plymouth sits on the southern coast of Devon, where the River Plym meets the English Channel, and its natural harbour has been a gateway to the world for centuries. It is famously the departure point of the Mayflower in 1620, when the first group of Pilgrims set sail for North America. Today the city blends maritime heritage with a lively waterfront: you can wander along the historic Barbican, explore the National Marine Aquarium, and enjoy fresh seafood in bustling cafés while the modern shopping precincts and the iconic Smeaton’s Tower lighthouse remind you that Plymouth is both a historic port and a vibrant, contemporary destination.

pna.name: Patna
pna.text: Patna, the capital of Bihar in eastern India, sits on the south bank of the wide Ganges River and has been a centre of Indian life for millennia. Known in ancient times as Pataliputra, it was the capital of the Mauryan Empire under Emperor Ashoka, who built a famous stone pillar that still stands in the city. Today Patna blends its historic aura with lively street life: bustling bazaars sell everything from silk saris to spicy snacks, the Bihar Museum showcases artefacts spanning pre-historic to modern times, and the expansive Gandhi Maidan offers a green respite where locals gather for concerts, fairs and evening walks.

pnq.name: Pune
pnq.text: Pune, a bustling city in the western state of Maharashtra, lies on the Deccan Plateau about 150 km southeast of Mumbai. It grew from the 17th-century Maratha stronghold of Shivaji’s son, who established the city as a centre of administration and learning. Today Pune mixes old and new: leafy avenues are lined with historic forts, colonial-era buildings and lively markets, while modern cafés, tech parks and universities give it a youthful, cosmopolitan vibe. Visitors can explore the tranquil Osho Garden, sample street-food delicacies such as misal pav, and enjoy the pleasant climate that makes strolling through its streets pleasant year-round.

poa.name: Porto Alegre
poa.text: Porto Alegre lies on the eastern bank of the Guaíba estuary in southern Brazil, at the foothills of the Serra Gaúcha. Founded in 1769 as a Portuguese military outpost, it later became the capital of the state of Rio Grande do Sul and a key centre for the gaucho culture that blends European, Indigenous and African influences. Today the city feels lively and cosmopolitan, with tree-lined avenues, bustling cafés and a vibrant arts scene; the historic centre offers colonial architecture, while the waterfront parks provide relaxed views of the water and a chance to sample the region’s famous barbecues and wine.

por.name: Portsmouth
por.text: Portsmouth is a bustling coastal city on the southern coast of England, set on a natural harbour at the tip of the Langstone Peninsula in Hampshire. It has a rich naval heritage; the world-famous HMS Victory, Admiral Nelson’s flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar, still lies in the historic dockyard. Today the city blends maritime history with a lively waterfront: you can wander the historic streets, explore museums and the modern shopping precinct, enjoy fresh seafood by the sea, and catch ferries to the Isle of Wight, all under a backdrop of striking Victorian architecture and vibrant waterfront parks.

rak.name: Marrakech
rak.text: Marrakech, situated in the western foothills of the Atlas Mountains in southern Morocco, has been a centre of trade and culture since it was founded in the 11th century by the Almoravid dynasty. The city's historic medina, a UNESCO World-heritage site, still contains the famous Koutoubia Mosque and the lively Jemaa el-Fna square, where storytellers, musicians and food stalls create a sensory feast each evening. Today visitors can wander narrow souks selling spices, textiles and ceramics, enjoy rooftop cafés overlooking the red-sandstone walls, and take short trips to nearby gardens and desert landscapes, making it a memorable stop on any North-African itinerary.

rec.name: Recife
rec.text: Recife, the capital of Pernambuco on Brazil’s north-eastern Atlantic coast, sits where the Capibaribe River meets the sea and is criss-crossed by a network of historic waterways. In the 17th century the city was seized by the Dutch, who held it from 1630 until the Portuguese reconquest in 1654, leaving a legacy of forts and Dutch-style architecture in the neighbourhood of Recife Antigo. Today visitors can stroll along colourful colonial streets, watch the sunrise over Boa Viagem beach, sample lively frevo music in the streets, and enjoy riverside cafés while watching colourful boats glide through the canals.

rnd.name: Rostov-on-Don
rnd.text: Rostov-on-Don sits on the western bank of the Don River in southern Russia, a gateway to the vast steppe and the Black Sea coast. Founded in the mid-18th century as a fortress to protect the empire’s southern frontier, it grew into a bustling trade hub and today it buzzes with a lively mix of history and modernity. Visitors can wander the wide embankment lined with cafés, explore the striking Rostov Kremlin and its golden domes, and soak up the vibrant atmosphere of markets selling everything from fresh fish to traditional crafts, all under a warm, sun-lit sky.

ros.name: Roscoff
ros.text: Roscoff is a charming fishing port on the north-west coast of Brittany, France, facing the English Channel and just a short ferry ride from Plymouth. Founded in the Middle Ages, the town became famous in the 19th century as the departure point for the first regular trans-Channel steamship service, linking France and Britain. Today Roscoff delights visitors with its colourful harbour, slate-roofed houses and a bustling market where fresh seafood and the celebrated “Roscoff pink” seaweed are sold. Stroll along the promenade, explore the historic granite church and sample the local cider for a quintessential Breton experience.

rot.name: Rotterdam
rot.text: Rotterdam sits on the banks of the Nieuwe Maas in the western Netherlands, just a short train ride from The Hague and a half-hour from the North Sea coast. The city rose from the ashes after World War II when its historic centre was heavily bombed, prompting a bold rebuild that gave Rotterdam its striking modern skyline. Today, visitors can wander along the bustling waterfront, admire daring architecture such as the cube houses and Erasmus Bridge, and enjoy a lively mix of multicultural cafés, bustling markets and world-class museums, all set against the backdrop of the busy port that is the heart of Europe's shipping trade.

rou.name: Rouen
rou.text: Rouen, perched on the River Seine in north-western France, is the historic capital of Normandy, roughly an hour and a half by train from Paris. It was here in 1419 that Joan of Arc was tried and later executed, a moment that still haunts the city’s medieval streets. Today the town blends cobbled alleys and half-timbered houses with bustling cafés, a vibrant arts scene and impressive Gothic architecture such as the towering Notre-Dame Cathedral that famously inspired Monet’s series of paintings. A stroll through its markets, museums and riverfront promenades feels both timeless and lively.

rsl.name: Rosslare
rsl.text: Rosslare, perched on the south-eastern tip of County Wexford, looks out over the Atlantic and the narrow St Gillian’s Strait that separates Ireland from Wales. The town grew around Rosslare Harbour, which was opened in 1906 to serve the new steam-packet service to Fishguard and still handles daily ferries to Pembroke Dock. Today the harbour area is a bustling gateway for travelers, while the adjoining sandy beach and flat promenade invite leisurely strolls, and a handful of cosy cafés and traditional pubs offer a relaxed taste of coastal life.

rtr.name: Rotorua
rtr.text: Rotorua, situated in the heart of New Zealand’s North Island within the Bay of Plenty region and set on the southern shore of Lake Rotorua, has been a centre of Māori life for centuries, home to the Te Arawa iwi. European visitors arrived in the 1860s and the town was declared a tourist resort in 1882, recognising its dramatic geysers and sulphur springs. Today the city blends geothermal landscapes, thriving Māori cultural performances, lake-front cafés and adventure activities, making it a lively destination for travellers seeking natural wonder and authentic New Zealand hospitality.

sal.name: Salisbury
sal.text: Salisbury is a historic market city set on the River Avon in the heart of Wiltshire, about 80 miles west of London and a short drive south from the stone circles of Stonehenge. Founded in Saxon times, it became famous in the 13th century for its magnificent cathedral, which boasts the tallest spire in England and houses the original Magna Carta. Today the city feels relaxed yet lively, with its medieval streets lined with independent shops, cozy cafés and a bustling market hall; the cathedral’s clock tower offers sweeping views of the surrounding countryside, making a visit both scenic and steeped in history.

san.name: Santander
san.text: Santander, perched on the northern coast of Spain in the autonomous community of Cantabria, is a lively seaside town overlooking the Bay of Biscay. Founded by the Romans as Portus Victoriae, it later became an important port for the Spanish crown, and its historic centre still shows the influence of 19th-century expansion under Queen María de las Mercedes. Today the city mixes elegant Art-Deco architecture with a bustling promenade, golden beaches and a vibrant culinary scene centred on fresh anchovies and local cheeses. Visitors can stroll along the Magdalena Peninsula, explore the maritime museum and enjoy the relaxed, salty air of this charming coastal gem.

sbh.name: Sabha
sbh.text: Sabha is a town in the far-south of Libya, sitting on the edge of the Sahara near the borders with Niger and Chad. It grew around a caravan stop on the historic trade routes that linked the Mediterranean coast with sub-Saharan Africa, and in the early twentieth century it became a centre for the trans-Saharan ivory and slave trade before those practices were outlawed. Today the town is a modest, sun-baked settlement where palm-shaded markets sell dates and textiles, the surrounding desert offers striking sand dunes for day-trips, and a small museum displays artefacts from its trading past.

sdg.name: San Diego
sdg.text: San Diego lies on the southern coast of California, bordering the Pacific Ocean and just a short drive from the Mexican border. Founded as a Spanish mission in 1769, the city grew around the historic Presidio and became a key naval base in the 20th century. Today it feels relaxed yet vibrant, with sun-kissed beaches, a bustling waterfront at the Embarcadero, and a mix of cultural attractions from the lively Gaslamp Quarter to the world-class museums of Balboa Park. Warm weather, friendly locals and endless outdoor activities make it a pleasant stop for any traveller.

sev.name: Seville
sev.text: Seville, situated on the banks of the Guadalquivir in the heart of Andalusia, was known to the Romans as Hispalis and later became the dazzling capital of Moorish Al-Andalus, its grand Giralda originally a minaret. Today the city blends its grand cathedral, the world’s largest Gothic church, with a lively tapas bar scene, bustling orange-tree lined plazas and nightly flamenco performances, while the annual Feria de Abril fills the streets with colour and music, making it a vibrant crossroads of history and modern Spanish life and warm hospitality for all.

sju.name: San Juan
sju.text: San Juan, the capital of Puerto Rico, sits on the island’s north-eastern coast overlooking the Atlantic. Founded by Spanish colonists in 1521, the city grew around the fortified walls of Old San Juan, where the 16th-century Castillo San Felipe del Morro and the massive San Cristóbal fort still dominate the skyline. Today it blends historic cobblestones with a waterfront, trendy cafés and an arts scene, while its beaches and colourful street life attract visitors from around the world. The mix of colonial charm and energy makes it an unforgettable destination.

slc.name: Salt Lake City
slc.text: Salt Lake City lies in the north-western corner of the United States, nestled at the foot of the Wasatch Mountains and alongside the great Great Salt Lake in Utah. Founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young, it quickly grew into a hub for westward settlers and the trans-continental railroad. Today the city blends modern skyscrapers with historic temples, offering easy access to outdoor adventures such as skiing, hiking and lake-side cycling, while its lively downtown boasts museums, a vibrant food scene and a welcoming, laid-back atmosphere.

smf.name: Sacramento
smf.text: Sacramento, the capital city of California, sits where the Sacramento and American Rivers meet in the heart of the state's fertile Central Valley. It grew rapidly during the Gold Rush, becoming the state capital in 1854 and preserving much of its 19th-century charm in the cobbled streets of Old Sacramento. Today the city offers a pleasant mix of history and modernity: riverfront parks invite picnics and kayaking, a lively farm-to-table restaurant scene showcases local produce, and museums such as the California State Railroad Museum and the Crocker Art Museum provide engaging cultural stops, all set against a backdrop of sunny skies and friendly locals.

sou.name: Southampton
sou.text: Southampton, a port city on England’s south-coast, lies on the northern shore of the Solent where the River Itchen meets the sea. It is famous as the departure point for the RMS Titanic in 1912, a historic moment that still echoes in the city's maritime museums. Today the waterfront buzzes with a mix of modern waterfront bars, historic dockside warehouses and the vibrant cultural quarter around the old medieval walls. Visitors can wander the bustling market, explore the SeaCity Museum, enjoy a stroll along the historic Ocean Village marina, and take a short ferry ride to the Isle of Wight, all set against a backdrop of lively cafés and a friendly, bustling atmosphere.

srg.name: Sorong
srg.text: Sorong – perched on the western tip of New Guinea, this bustling port city greets you where the warm waters of the Raja Ampat archipelago meet the vast expanse of the Pacific. Once a modest Dutch outpost in the early 1900s, Sorong grew into a strategic gateway during World War II and later became the commercial heart of West Papua. Today it pulses with modern energy: a hub for oil and gas, a launchpad for divers diving into world‑renowned coral reefs, and a cultural crossroads where indigenous traditions mingle with vibrant street markets.
