Join us as we explore the charm and promise of Sorong, Indonesia’s hidden coastal gem.

stl.name: St Louis
stl.text: St Louis lies on the western bank of the Mississippi River in the heart of the American Midwest, about 300 miles west of the Illinois border. Founded in 1764 by French fur traders, the city grew around the historic Gateway Arch, a 630-foot stainless-steel monument that commemorates the westward expansion of the United States. Today visitors can stroll along the vibrant Riverfront, explore world-class museums such as the St Louis Art Museum and the Science Centre, and savour famous barbecue in the bustling downtown districts, all while enjoying the city’s blend of historic brick warehouses and modern skyline.

str.name: Strasbourg
str.text: Strasbourg, perched on the banks of the River Ill where France meets Germany, is the capital of the Alsace region in north-eastern France. Founded as a Roman settlement, it later became an Imperial Free City of the Holy Roman Empire and was a key centre of the Reformation, hosting the famous 1529 Diet of Augsburg delegates. Today the city charms visitors with its UNESCO-listed Grande Île, where the timber-framed “half-timber” houses line cobbled streets and the stunning Gothic cathedral towers above the bustling markets. A blend of French and German cuisine, lively cafés and modern European institutions makes Strasbourg a vibrant, walkable destination.

tao.name: Qingdao
tao.text: Qingdao, a coastal city in Shandong province on China’s Yellow Sea, is famed for its blend of German colonial heritage and modern seaside charm. Founded as a fishing village, it became a German concession in 1898, which left the striking red-tiled roofs of the former Governor’s Hall and the historic Badaguan neighbourhood. Today visitors can stroll along the bustling waterfront promenade, sip locally brewed Tsingtao beer in lively pubs, wander the fragrant jasmine-lined streets, and enjoy fresh seafood while taking in the backdrop of gentle hills and crystal-clear bays.

tfs.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife
tfs.text: Santa Cruz de Tenerife – perched on the northeast coast of Spain’s sun‑kissed Canary Islands, this vibrant city greets you with volcanic horizons and Atlantic breezes. Founded in the 16th century as a modest port for sugar and wine, it soon blossomed into a bustling gateway for explorers heading to the New World. Today, Santa Cruz is the archipelago’s political and cultural heart, famed for its colorful Carnaval, bustling Mercado de Nuestra Señora de África, and striking modern architecture like the Auditorio de Tenerife. From historic plazas to lively waterfront cafés, the city perfectly blends heritage with contemporary island charm.

tls.name: Toulouse
tls.text: Toulouse, in southwestern France, lies on the banks of the Garonne River about 150 km east of the Atlantic coast. Known as “La Ville Rose” for its distinctive pink-hued bricks, the city was a centre of medieval commerce and later became a hub of the aerospace industry, home to the headquarters of Airbus. Visitors today can wander its historic centre, admire the towering Saint-Sernin basilica, and relax in lively cafés lining the riverfront, while the modern university atmosphere adds a youthful buzz to the charming, sun-lit streets.

tof.name: Tomsk
tof.text: Tomsk lies in western Siberia, on the banks of the Tom River about 650 km east of the Ural Mountains and roughly 2 000 km northeast of Moscow. Founded in 1604 as a fort on the Siberian trade route, it is one of the oldest towns in the region and today hosts Russia’s first university, established in 1888. Visitors find a lively mix of historic wooden houses, leafy avenues and modern cafés, while the riverfront offers pleasant walks and occasional boat trips. Museums, theatres and a vibrant student community give the city a youthful, cultural buzz that contrasts pleasantly with its frontier heritage.

tou.name: Tours
tou.text: Tours, set on the gentle bend of the River Loire in the heart of France’s historic Centre-Val de Loire, is a lively gateway to the country’s famed châteaux. Its medieval old town grew around the impressive Saint-Gatien cathedral, which dates back to the 12th century and bears the marks of the Hundred Years’ War. Today the city blends that rich heritage with a bustling, contemporary vibe: cobbled streets are lined with cafés and boutique shops, the vibrant market on Place Plumereau hums with locals, and river cruises offer relaxed views of the surrounding vineyards. Tours feels both comfortably historic and refreshingly modern, making it a pleasant stop for any traveller.

tpa.name: Tampa
tpa.text: Tampa sits on the western edge of Florida, straddling the Hillsborough River where it meets the Gulf of Mexico, and is the largest city in the Tampa Bay area. The settlement began as Fort Brooke in 1824, later growing into a bustling port and, in the late-19th century, becoming famous for its thriving cigar factories in Ybor City, a neighbourhood founded by Cuban and Spanish immigrants. Today the city offers a lively mix of modern skyline, waterfront parks and a lively historic quarter, while nearby sandy beaches, Busch Gardens and a diverse food scene make a visit both relaxed and exciting.

tsn.name: Tianjin
tsn.text: Tianjin, a bustling port city in northern China, sits on the banks of the Hai River about 120 kilometres southeast of Beijing. It grew into a major treaty port after the Opium Wars, when foreign concessions were established in the 19th century, leaving a distinctive mix of European-style architecture and traditional Chinese streets. Today the city blends sleek skyscrapers with historic districts such as the Italian-style St Leonardo’s Avenue, offering lively food markets, river cruises, and modern art galleries. Visitors can savour fresh seafood, wander the colourful hutongs and enjoy a vibrant nightlife that reflects both its rich past and its fast-moving present.

tus.name: Tucson
tus.text: Tucson, nestled in the southern part of Arizona about 60 miles north of the Mexican border, lies at the edge of the Sonoran Desert and is framed by the Santa Catalina, Rincon and Tucson Mountains. The town began as a Spanish presidio in 1775, making it one of the oldest European-settled communities in the American Southwest. Today the city blends desert scenery with a lively cultural scene: you can wander historic Fourth Avenue, explore the University of Arizona’s museums, admire towering saguaro cacti in Saguaro National Park, and enjoy a thriving food and arts scene that feels both relaxed and surprisingly cosmopolitan.

tzx.name: Trabzon
tzx.text: Trabzon sits on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey, framed by lush hills and the Pontic Mountains. Founded as the Greek colony Trapezus in the 8th century BC, it later became an important stop on the Silk Road and the site of the famous Sumela Monastery, perched on a cliff overlooking the surrounding forest. Today the city offers a pleasant mix of sea-front promenades, lively fish markets and Ottoman-era tea houses where you can sample the local Black Sea tea. The backdrop of mist-y mountains and the scent of fresh seafood make a visit both relaxing and memorable.

ufa.name: Ufa
ufa.text: Ufa, the capital of Bashkortostan in the western foothills of the Ural Mountains, sits on the banks of the Belaya River about 1,200 km east of Moscow. Founded in 1574 as a Russian fortress, it later became an important centre for oil production in the early 20th century, shaping its industrial heritage. Today the city blends Soviet-era architecture with vibrant cultural life: you can stroll along the river promenade, explore the colourful Bashkir State Museum, and sample hearty Tatar and Bashkir cuisine in bustling cafés, while the surrounding hills offer easy hikes and a refreshing contrast to the urban bustle.

val.name: Valencia
val.text: Valencia, Spain, sits on the eastern Mediterranean coast where the Turia River meets the sea, about three hours by train south of Barcelona. Founded as a Roman colony in the second century BC, the city later flourished under Moorish rule and retained its medieval walls, parts of which you can still see strolling through the historic centre. Today Valencia feels vibrant and laid-back: you can wander the futuristic City of Arts and Sciences, sip a chilled horchata in a sun-dappled plaza, or wander the bustling Central Market, all while the scent of paella drifting from seaside restaurants reminds you why this port city is a favourite stop for travellers.

xmn.name: Xiamen
xmn.text: Xiamen, a bustling coastal city in Fujian province on China’s southeast seaboard, sits opposite the Taiwan Strait and is linked to the historic Gulangyu Island by a short ferry ride. It became a treaty port in the mid-19th century after the First Opium War, which sparked its development as a centre of overseas trade. Today the city charms visitors with palm-shaded promenades, a lively pedestrian street full of street food stalls, well-preserved temples and modern cafés, and a pleasant subtropical climate that makes exploring its harbourside parks and colourful neighbourhoods a relaxed delight.

yfc.name: Fredericton
yfc.text: Fredericton, the capital city of New Brunswick, lies on the banks of the Saint John River in the heart of the province’s western valley. Founded in 1785 and named after Prince Frederick, the town grew around a Loyalist settlement and later became a centre for the province’s timber trade, a heritage still hinted at in its historic wooden warehouses. Today visitors can stroll along the riverfront promenade, explore the striking Legislative Assembly building and vibrant downtown filled with galleries, cafés and the University of New Brunswick campus, all set against a backdrop of leafy parks and gentle river views.

yks.name: Yakutsk
yks.text: Yakutsk, perched on the banks of the Lena River in the heart of Siberia, is the capital of the Sakha Republic and one of the world’s coldest cities, where winter temperatures regularly plunge below –40 °C. Founded in 1632 as a Russian outpost, it grew into a centre for the fur trade and later for diamond mining, which still fuels the local economy. Today the town is a surprising blend of modernity and tradition: colourful wooden houses line lively streets, museums showcase indigenous Yakut culture, and a hearty cuisine of reindeer and fish warms visitors after a crisp, clear-air stroll beneath snow-capped hills.

yok.name: Yokohama
yok.text: Yokohama, the bustling port city just a half‑hour train ride south of Tokyo, greets travelers with a perfect blend of sea‑sprayed charm and modern flair. Founded as a modest fishing village, it exploded onto the world stage in 1859 when the Treaty of Kanagawa opened its harbor to foreign trade, sparking the iconic Red Brick Warehouses and the lively foreign‑settlement vibe that still lingers today. Today, Yokohama is Japan’s second‑largest city, a hub of technology, fashion and gastronomy—home to the towering Landmark Tower, the serene Sankeien Garden, and a famed Chinatown that serves up some of the country’s best dumplings. Join us as we explore this dynamic gateway between tradition and tomorrow.

yor.name: York
yor.text: York, a historic city in North Yorkshire, lies at the confluence of the Rivers Ouse and Foss, about 30 miles north-east of Leeds and 190 miles north of London. Founded by the Romans as Eboracum, it later became a key Viking-era centre and the site of the famous medieval York Minster. Today the walled city feels compact and lively: you can wander the cobbled Shambles, explore the National Railway Museum, and enjoy the vibrant cafés and independent shops that spill onto the ancient streets, while the impressive city walls offer pleasant walks with views over the modern town below.

yqr.name: Regina
yqr.text: Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan in Canada, sits on the flat, golden prairie plain about 190 kilometres south of the province’s northern border and 250 kilometres north of the United States. The city grew from a railway settlement founded in 1882 and was promptly chosen as the provincial capital, a status it retains today. Its most striking landmark is the grand sandstone Legislative Building, whose copper dome can be seen from many points in town. Modern visitors find a friendly, laid-back atmosphere, with excellent museums, a vibrant culinary scene and wide-open riverfront parks that showcase the sweeping skies and endless horizons of the Canadian West.

yqt.name: Thunder Bay
yqt.text: Thunder Bay sits on the north-western shore of Lake Superior in Ontario, Canada, where the Kaministiquia River meets the lake’s vast waters. The city grew from the historic fur-trading outpost of Fort William, a key Hudson’s Bay Company centre in the early 1800s that helped open the interior to European trade. Today the town blends rugged natural beauty with a relaxed, welcoming vibe: you can stroll along the waterfront boardwalk, explore the striking rock formations of the nearby Sleeping Giant, enjoy Indigenous art galleries and sample fresh lake fish in cosy cafés, all under a backdrop of striking shoreline and pine-clad hills.

yxe.name: Saskatoon
yxe.text: Saskatoon sits on the east bank of the South Saskatchewan River in the central part of the Canadian province of Saskatchewan, roughly midway between Calgary and Winnipeg. Founded in the late 19th century, the town grew around a North West Company trading post and was officially incorporated in 1906, becoming a key hub for grain and railway traffic on the Canadian Prairies. Today visitors find a vibrant mix of modern cafés, art galleries and riverside parks, with the striking skyline reflected in the river’s waters and a lively cultural scene that celebrates both its Indigenous heritage and its pioneering past.

yxy.name: Whitehorse
yxy.text: Whitehorse, the capital of Yukon in north-west Canada, sits on the banks of the mighty Yukon River about 30 kilometres south of the Alaska border. It grew from a modest river-crossing called “the White Horse Rapids” into a bustling supply hub during the Klondike Gold Rush of the late 1890s, when prospectors streamed through on their way to the goldfields. Today the town blends frontier charm with modern comforts: colourful storefronts line Main Street, the Yukon Beringia Interpretive Centre showcases ancient fossils, and the surrounding mountains and river offer spectacular hiking, wildlife spotting and, in winter, brilliant aurora borealis displays.

yyg.name: Charlottetown
yyg.text: Charlottetown, the capital of Prince Edward Island, sits on the southern shore of the island at the head of Charlottetown Harbour, where the Northumberland Strait meets the Gulf of St Lawrence. In 1864 the town hosted the Charlottetown Conference, the first meeting that set the foundations for Canadian Confederation, earning it the nickname “Birthplace of Confederation”. Today the city blends historic charm with a lively modern vibe: colourful Victorian houses line the waterfront, boutique shops and cafés spill onto pedestrian streets, and the bustling summer festivals fill the air with music and the scent of fresh seafood, making a visit both relaxed and culturally rich.

yzd.name: Yazd
yzd.text: Yazd, a desert city in central Iran about 250 km south-east of Tehran, sits on the edge of the Dasht-e Kavir plain. It is famous for its ancient mud-brick architecture and was a centre of Zoroastrian worship long before the Islamic era, with the historic Fahadan quarter preserving narrow alleys and wind-catchers that date back to the 12th century. Today the town feels calm and sun-warmed; you can wander its quiet bazaars, sip tea in a courtyard shaded by towering qanats, and watch the sunset turn the ochre roofs into a golden glow, while modern cafés and museums sit alongside the timeless adobe walls.

yzf.name: Yellowknife
yzf.text: Yellowknife, the capital of Canada’s Northwest Territories, sits on the northern shore of Great Slave Lake, just below the Arctic Circle. Founded in the 1930s during the region’s gold-rush, the town was named after the Yellowknife Dene, whose traditional lands include the area. Today the city is a vibrant mix of modern amenities and wilderness adventure, offering museums that showcase Indigenous culture and mining history, colourful waterfront promenades, and easy access to spectacular northern lights, dog-sledding and canoe trips on the lake, all set against a backdrop of boreal forest and crisp, clean air.

zar.name: Zaragoza
zar.text: Zaragoza, nestled in the north-east of Spain on the banks of the Ebro River, lies roughly halfway between Madrid and Barcelona and serves as the capital of the autonomous community of Aragon. The city’s most famous landmark, the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar, has been a major pilgrimage site since the early medieval period, when legend says the Virgin Mary appeared to the apostle James here. Today Zaragoza buzzes with a lively mix of historic charm and modern energy: you can stroll through bustling tapas bars, explore the Roman-era Aljafería Palace, and enjoy riverside walks while the city’s vibrant cultural calendar offers festivals, music and art throughout the year.
